correctness.rationale: Dihedral symmetry reduces x to one reference edge. On E0 the sum chord has norm 2 while the difference chord is shorter. On E1 the sum norm is max{sqrt(2)+da,2-db}>=sqrt(2), while the difference norm is <=sqrt(2), with equality only at the shared quarter-turn endpoint. On E2 the two chords reduce, after coordinate symmetry, to N(sqrt(2)+d(a-b),w) and N(sqrt(2)-d(a-b),w); since |w|<=d and the first coordinate is always larger than |w|, the norm is strictly increasing in that coordinate, so equality is exactly a=b, i.e. y=Rx. E3 has the reversed sqrt(2) inequalities with only the other shared endpoint. Central symmetry supplies E4--E7 and gives the second family y=-Rx. Substitution then gives both chord norms sqrt(2).
risks: Endpoint points belong to two closed polygonal edges; the proof explicitly identifies those duplicate zeros with the E2/E6 quarter-turn families.
The exact-grid checker is supplementary; the continuum classification is carried by the analytic edge inequalities in RESULT.md.

originality.rationale: Targeted published-finding corpus searches covered the exact isosceles condition, regular-octagon aliases, quarter-turn/rotation language, and James-type terminology. No covering statement was located. The closest indexed regular-octagon records concern von Neumann--Jordan profiles and unit-separation angle moduli, not the equality locus N(x+y)=N(x-y). The current and immediate-prior own ledgers were checked. An own universal J_2 identity covers only the scalar supremum, an H_2 result concerns a scaled rotation optimization, and an Omega result gives a different isosceles objective; none implies the full orthogonality graph. The inspected primary literature introduces isosceles-based constants and proves general attainment relations but does not state the regular-octagon quarter-turn classification.

An equivalent classification may exist under a linearly equivalent octagon normalization or orthogonality-graph terminology.

value.rationale: The result is a complete natural classification of a classical orthogonality relation on a canonical non-Hilbert polygonal norm, not a single optimized number. It shows that the regular octagon has a rigid unit isosceles-orthogonality graph consisting of exactly two quarter-turn partners per point and that every admissible symmetric chord has one common length. This structural information is stronger than known scalar James-type extrema and can serve as an exact benchmark for comparing isosceles-based geometric constants on polygonal Banach planes.
risks: The theorem does not yet identify which other regular polygons, if any, share this rigidity.
